shots.title: Your new 1 TB drive
shots.narration: You buy a one-terabyte drive. You plug it in. {p} And your computer says nine hundred thirty-one gigabytes. {pp} Sixty-nine gigabytes, gone. {p} So who's lying? The box, or your computer?

Neither. Both numbers are correct. {p} They're counting in two different units, and both units are called a gigabyte. {p} And once you see how that happened, you'll spot the same trick in your RAM, in your internet bill, and inside your SSD, which actually holds more than one terabyte. {pp} You just can't use it.

items.text: Your SSD holds MORE than 1 TB

shots.title: powers of two
shots.narration: It starts with how computers count. {p} Everything inside is binary, so memory comes in powers of two: two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two. {p} And two to the tenth power is one thousand and twenty-four. {p} That's so close to one thousand that early computer engineers just started calling it a kilo.

shots.src: Binary addressing: n address lines → 2ⁿ locations
shots.label: 10 address wires
shots.sub: each one is a 1 or a 0 → 2¹⁰ = 1,024 addresses
shots.narration: There's a physical reason for those powers of two. {p} A memory chip finds each byte by its address, sent over wires, and every wire is either a one or a zero. {p} With ten wires, you can name exactly one thousand and twenty-four addresses. Not one thousand. {p} So memory naturally comes in sizes like one thousand twenty-four, two thousand forty-eight, four thousand ninety-six.

react.at: either a one or a zero

shots.title: Same prefix, two meanings
shots.narration: The problem is that the small difference doesn't stay small. {p} At kilo, the binary version is two point four percent bigger. At mega, it's almost five percent. At giga, seven point four. {p} And at tera, the gap is ten percent. {pp} Every step up, the two meanings drift further apart.

shots.title: the math on your drive
shots.narration: Now let's do the math on your drive. {p} The box means a terabyte in the official sense: one trillion bytes. {p} Windows divides that by a binary gigabyte, which is one billion, seventy-three million and change. {p} One trillion divided by that is nine hundred thirty-one point three. {pp} Not a single byte is missing. {p} Windows is measuring in binary gigabytes, and still calling them gigabytes.

lines.note: bytes, as printed on the box

shots.src: BIPM (SI prefixes, 1960); IEC 60027-2 Amd. 2 (1998); Apple, Mac OS X 10.6 (2009)
shots.title: So who's right?
shots.narration: So who's right? {p} Technically, the drive makers. In the metric system, giga has meant one billion since 1960. {p} In 1998, the International Electrotechnical Commission even created new names for the binary units: kibibyte, mebibyte, gibibyte. {p} Almost nobody says them out loud. {p} Windows kept the old names. {p} And Apple went the other way: since 2009, a Mac counts storage in thousands.

shots.title: Same drive, same bytes
shots.narration: Same drive, same bytes. {p} Plug it into a Windows PC and it says nine hundred thirty-one gigabytes. {p} Plug it in on a Mac, and it says one thousand. {pp} The only thing that changed is the ruler.

shots.src: Redmond Magazine (28 Jun 2006); The Register (2 Nov 2007)
shots.title: Gigabytes in court
shots.narration: This confusion has actually ended up in court. {p} In 2006, Western Digital settled a class action that said its eighty-gigabyte drive showed up as about seventy-four. {p} It gave customers free backup software, and paid half a million dollars in legal fees. {p} In 2007, Seagate settled a similar case: five percent cash back on older drives, or free software. {pp} Neither company admitted doing anything wrong. {p} And both kept using the decimal gigabyte. They just print the definition on the box now.

shots.title: the 3.5-inch floppy disk
shots.narration: But the strangest gigabyte cousin is older. {p} The classic floppy disk said one point four four megabytes. {p} It held one million, four hundred seventy-four thousand, five hundred and sixty bytes. {p} That's fourteen forty times one thousand twenty-four. {p} So that megabyte was a thousand binary kilobytes. {pp} Half decimal, half binary. It's not a real megabyte in either system.

shots.src: Inherent SSD over-provisioning: binary NAND vs decimal capacity (TechTarget, Kingston)
shots.title: Inside a typical 1 TB SSD
shots.sub: flash chips are built in binary sizes: 1,024 GiB
shots.narration: Now, the twist I promised. {p} Flash memory chips are built in binary sizes. A typical one-terabyte SSD contains one thousand and twenty-four binary gigabytes of flash. {p} That's about one thousand ninety-nine regular gigabytes. {p} But it's sold, and shown, as one terabyte. {pp} So about a hundred gigabytes is hidden. On purpose.

shots.src: TechTarget: SSD over-provisioning; Kingston: Understanding SSD Over-provisioning
shots.title: What the hidden space does
shots.narration: Flash memory wears out. Each cell can only be erased so many times. {p} So the drive's controller keeps that hidden space for itself: to spread writes evenly across the chips, to clean up old data in the background, and to replace cells that die. {p} The industry calls this overprovisioning. {pp} Your drive isn't hiding space from you. {p} It's hiding it for you, so it lasts longer.

items.text: spare blocks for cells that die

shots.title: your internet plan
shots.narration: And there's one more unit trap, and you probably pay for it every month. {p} Internet speed is sold in bits per second. Files are measured in bytes. And one byte is eight bits. {p} So a one-gigabit connection downloads at most one hundred twenty-five megabytes per second, before any overhead. {pp} Little b, big B. {p} One letter, a factor of eight.

shots.title: your RAM
shots.src: JEDEC memory convention: 1 GB of RAM = 2³⁰ bytes
shots.narration: Meanwhile, RAM is still sold in binary. {p} A sixteen-gigabyte memory stick really holds sixteen binary gigabytes: about seventeen point two billion bytes. {p} So the word gigabyte means one billion bytes on your drive, about one point oh seven billion in your RAM, {p} and on your internet bill, it's not even bytes.

So, your drive isn't lying. {p} The box speaks metric. Windows speaks binary, using metric words. {p} Nine hundred thirty-one gigabytes and one terabyte are the same trillion bytes, measured with two different rulers. {p} And the lesson goes way beyond hard drives: {pp} whenever you see a number, check the unit.

next.title: Tiny math errors that cost lives

shots.narration: And if you want to see what happens when a number doesn't fit its box, watch this one next: four tiny math errors that cost lives and millions. {p} I'm How It Ticks. See you in the next one.

You buy a 1 TB drive and your PC shows 931 GB. Nothing is missing: "gigabyte" means two different things. Why computers count in 1,024s, who's actually right, the lawsuits it caused, the weird 1.44 MB floppy, and why your SSD secretly holds MORE than 1 TB.
